title: If you're a Brahmin
hook: Kabir asks, if birth made you high, why weren't you born by some other road (Gauri, Kabir, ang 324)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the qazi, and your line, the elephant bowed. Did you stand still for one breath before something big? Today Kabir stands his ground with words. Day seven hundred fifty-two.

A question can do what an argument can't. Ask someone, where were you born, and you learn a city. Ask, how were you born, and everyone in the room gives the same answer. Same way in. Same cry. Same small, wet, helpless start. A weaver in Kashi once took that plain fact and turned it into a question for a learned man who thought his birth made him higher. The question is still sitting in the Guru Granth Sahib, in Raag Gauri, waiting for whoever reads it. Today: if you're a Brahmin.
screen: `WHERE WERE YOU BORN?` → `HOW WERE YOU BORN?` → `THE SAME WAY IN.`

segments.voice: Kabir starts in the womb. In the womb, he says, there's no family line and no caste. Everyone comes from the same seed of the Divine. Then he turns to the pandit, the learned man, and asks: tell me, since when have you been a Brahmin? Don't waste your life just saying the word. And then the question from today's title. If you're a Brahmin, born of a Brahmin mother, why didn't you come into the world by some other road? He presses it with a picture. How are you a Brahmin and I a Shudra? Is it blood in my veins and milk in yours? You can hear the weaver's humor in it. He isn't shouting. He's asking a question so plain that pride has nowhere to stand. Now the part that keeps this from being an attack on anyone. Kabir doesn't throw away the word Brahmin. He gives it a new meaning. The hymn ends: Kabir says, whoever reflects on God, that one we call a Brahmin. So the line isn't against a people or a faith. It's against the idea that birth decides worth. Sikhs hear this hymn beside the Gurus' own teaching, which also refused to rank people by caste, and beside the langar, where everyone sits on the same floor and eats the same food. Today's line is the fact Kabir starts from. Whatever titles come later, every one of us was born the same way.
screen: `IN THE WOMB, NO CASTE.` · `WHY NOT BY SOME OTHER ROAD?` · `BLOOD IN MINE, MILK IN YOURS?` · `WHOEVER REFLECTS ON GOD.` · then, large: `BORN THE SAME WAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: meet someone as an equal. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person you tend to look up to too much, or down on without noticing. A boss, a cleaner, a celebrity, a cousin. Picture them as Kabir does: arriving in the world the same way you did, small and crying. Hold that picture for a few breaths. Then picture them now, and see if anything has leveled out. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once for them and once for you. The bell holds the time.
Brahmin. Kabir's question to the proud, learned man: if birth made you one, why weren't you born by some other road?
Your line: born the same way. Today, greet one person you'd usually pass by, the same way you'd greet someone you admire. Day seven hundred fifty-two.

howItsDone: Sikhs sing this Gauri hymn of Kabir in kirtan, and teachers connect it with langar and the Gurus' rejection of caste, where all sit together on the floor and share one meal.

fork.setup: you're Kabir, a weaver. a learned man says his birth makes him higher than you. what do you do?
options: insult his family and his faith.
ask him a plain question about how he was born.
fork.reveal: Kabir asks: if you're a Brahmin, born of a Brahmin mother, why didn't you come by some other road? then he says whoever reflects on God is the Brahmin.

original.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi, as the hymn writes it: a Brahmin. Kabir keeps the word and gives it to whoever reflects on God.

trapdoor: what you thought: a saint picking a fight with priests.
what it means: a plain question about birth, so pride has nowhere to stand.
what a scholar hears: the hymn ends by redefining the Brahmin as whoever reflects on God, keeping the word and changing its meaning.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Raag Gauri, Kabir, Ang 324 (no caste in the womb; 'if you are a Brahmin born of a Brahmin mother'; blood and milk; whoever reflects on God)

notes: Hymn paraphrased throughout; confirm Ang 324 and the renderings, especially 'seed of the Divine' (brahm bind) and 'whoever reflects on God, that one we call a Brahmin'.
Framing: the hymn is presented as against birth-rank, not against Hindus or Brahmins; Kabir redefines the word rather than rejecting it. Confirm fairness.
Langar and the Gurus' rejection of caste: general Sikh teaching, not cited to a specific text; confirm.
Gurmukhi ਬ੍ਰਾਹਮਣੁ (with the final aunkar as in the hymn) and 'BRAAH-man': confirm.
Audit: read clean against Ang 324 (Gauri, Kabir); day 748's fork, which duplicated this day's fork, was rewritten there.
